cards.front: {{c1::Allodynia}} is pain from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain.
cards.quote: Allodynia is pain from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain.

cards.front: {{c1::Hyperalgesia}} is more pain to a stimulus that already hurts.
cards.quote: Hyperalgesia is more pain to a stimulus that already hurts.

cards.front: {{c1::Spontaneous pain}} is pain with no applied stimulus.
cards.why: No applied stimulus does not mean no neural cause: nerve fibres can fire on their own.
cards.quote: Spontaneous pain is pain with no applied stimulus.

cards.front: In a rodent von Frey assay, what is the paw-withdrawal threshold?
cards.back: The force that makes the paw lift, estimated over repeated trials; many labs use the force producing withdrawal half the time.
cards.quote: The withdrawal threshold is the force that makes the paw lift, estimated over repeated trials

cards.front: A researcher proposes that the microglia–spinal disinhibition chain from rodent nerve-injury studies explains persistent pain in arthritis. How should that claim be qualified?
cards.back: It is a hypothesis. Rule: these studies establish links in rodent nerve-injury models, not pain driven by ongoing tissue damage. In arthritis, ongoing input and changed processing can coexist.
cards.quote: or in pain driven by ongoing tissue damage, such as arthritis, where ongoing input and changed processing can coexist.

cards.front: An injured rat withdraws from weak von Frey filaments. A treatment reverses its mechanical allodynia-like hypersensitivity. What happens to the withdrawal-threshold curve, and why?
cards.back: The threshold rises toward baseline: stronger filaments are needed to trigger withdrawal. The assay measures reversal of reflex hypersensitivity; the effect may be temporary.
cards.quote: That last row is what every "reversed the allodynia" in this lesson means: the curve was pushed back up.
cards.section: The signature: a threshold that falls and stays down

cards.front: After rat L5 spinal nerve ligation and cutting, where did spontaneous activity develop within a day, and what does this show?
cards.back: About half of the C-fibre nociceptors in uninjured L4 developed spontaneous activity. Ectopic firing is not confined to injured afferents; uninjured neighbours can supply ongoing peripheral input without an applied stimulus.
cards.why: About half of the uninjured L4 C-fibre nociceptors developed spontaneous activity within a day in this preparation.
cards.quote: Rat models show that nerve injury changes both injured afferents and their uninjured neighbours.
cards.section: The ganglion that will not stop firing

cards.front: Seven days after L5 spinal nerve ligation in rats, a lab samples only the uninjured L4 ganglion and finds more Nav1.7. What should it expect in injured L5, and why?
cards.back: Less Nav1.7 mRNA and protein in L5 in this model. The direction depends on the ganglion sampled; the L4 increase cannot be generalized to injured fibres or other injury models.
cards.why: Expression is a different readout from firing; an expression change alone does not establish increased spontaneous activity.
cards.quote: Nav1.7 mRNA and protein fell in the injured L5 ganglion and rose in the adjacent, uninjured L4 ganglion.
cards.section: The ganglion that will not stop firing

cards.front: Cultured sensory neurons from human surgical ganglia fired spontaneously, associated with donors’ pain. Why does this not establish that ectopic firing caused their pain?
cards.back: It is an association in cultured cells. Dissociation cuts axons, and more than a day in culture makes dish firing only a proxy for activity in the body.
cards.quote: It is an association, and dissociation cuts every axon
cards.section: The ganglion that will not stop firing

cards.front: How does KCC2 help keep the anion reversal potential low in a lamina I neuron?
cards.back: It transports potassium and chloride out of the cell together.
cards.why: GABA and glycine synapses pull voltage toward the anion reversal potential; their channels also pass some bicarbonate.
cards.quote: That potential stays low because a transporter, KCC2, carries potassium and chloride out of the cell together.
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In a passive neuron at steady state with no injected current, what determines the membrane voltage?
cards.back: The conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials: V = Σ(gE)/Σg.
cards.quote: at steady state, with no current injected, the voltage sits at the conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials.
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In the passive lamina I model, why can a synapse depolarize a resting cell yet still oppose reaching spike threshold?
cards.back: It pulls voltage toward its reversal potential. If that potential remains below threshold, the synapse still increases the excitation needed to reach threshold.
cards.why: A depolarizing shift in E_anion describes the reversal potential, not necessarily a change in membrane voltage. Real neurons also depend on timing, location and active channels.
cards.quote: In this steady-state model the synapse adds to the excitation needed whenever E_anion is below threshold,
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: Use illustrative passive-model values: leak conductance 1 at −65 mV, inhibitory conductance 1 at E_anion = −70 mV, and touch conductance 0.4 at 0 mV. Calculate steady voltage and compare with threshold −50 mV.
cards.back: V = [1 × (−65) + 1 × (−70) + 0.4 × 0]/(1 + 1 + 0.4) = −56.2 mV, rounded. The steady voltage is below threshold.
cards.quote: For the healthy row, the balance point is (1 × −65 + 0.4 × 0 + 1 × −70) / (1 + 0.4 + 1) = −56.2 mV.
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In an illustrative passive model, leak conductance is 1 at −65 mV, excitation drives toward 0 mV, and threshold is −50 mV. Find the excitation needed at threshold with inhibitory conductance 1 at −55 mV, then with no inhibition.
cards.back: With inhibition, −50 = (−65 − 55)/(2 + g_exc), giving g_exc = 0.4. Without inhibition, −50 = −65/(1 + g_exc), giving 0.3. The depolarizing synapse still raises the required excitation.
cards.quote: yet it still raises the excitation needed to reach threshold (0.4 against 0.3 with no inhibition),
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In a passive neuron starting below threshold, a touch would bring steady voltage exactly to threshold. Does the model predict a finite-time threshold crossing, and what condition would allow one?
cards.back: No finite-time crossing is predicted at that boundary. The steady value must lie above threshold and the touch must last long enough; this passive model contains no spike mechanism.
cards.quote: Starting below threshold, the voltage crosses in real time only if the steady value lies above threshold and the touch lasts long enough.
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: At 37 °C, outside chloride stays fixed while intracellular chloride doubles. Using ΔE_Cl = 26.7 mV × ln([Cl⁻]in,new/[Cl⁻]in,old), calculate the reversal-potential shift.
cards.back: ΔE_Cl = 26.7 mV × ln 2 ≈ +18.5 mV: a depolarizing shift. This is the chloride reversal potential; bicarbonate also affects E_anion.
cards.quote: each doubling of chloride inside the cell makes the chloride reversal potential about 18.5 mV more positive (26.7 mV × ln 2).
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In rat nerve-injury studies, induced ATP-gated {{c1::P2X4}} receptors were found on reactive spinal microglia.
cards.quote: found that induced P2X4 receptors, channels opened by ATP, sat on reactive spinal microglia,
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In rats, lowering P2X4 suppressed tactile allodynia; transferring ATP-stimulated microglia into naive rats produced it. What was needed, and what was sufficient?
cards.back: P2X4 was needed for the tested allodynia; stimulated whole microglia were sufficient to induce it. Neither test establishes that P2X4 alone is sufficient.
cards.quote: The test of need was on a receptor, and the test of enough was on whole cells;
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In rat studies linking microglia to lamina I neurons, what BDNF–TrkB mechanism was supported by release measurements and signalling blockade?
cards.back: ATP-stimulated microglia released BDNF; BDNF acted through TrkB to depolarize E_anion. Blocking BDNF–TrkB signalling reversed both the shift and allodynia.
cards.quote: showed that ATP-stimulated microglia release BDNF, and that BDNF acting on TrkB receptors depolarizes the anion reversal potential
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: Rat studies support a P2X4 → BDNF → TrkB → shifted E_anion chain. Which further step connects that chain to a formerly ineffective touch driving a lamina I neuron, and what is its evidence level?
cards.back: Weaker inhibition lets touch input reach firing threshold in the model. Rule: raising E_anion toward threshold reduces the excitation needed. This step is a balance-point inference, not a direct touch-evoked recording in those papers.
cards.quote: that last step is an inference from the model and the definition of allodynia, not a recording in these papers.
cards.section: How a touch could now fire a pain neuron

cards.front: In rat dorsal-horn recordings seven days after spared nerve injury, mean spontaneous EPSC frequency was 15.9 Hz versus 9.0 Hz in sham animals. Calculate the absolute increase, fold change and percentage increase.
cards.back: Increase = 15.9 − 9.0 = 6.9 Hz. Fold change = 15.9/9.0 ≈ 1.77. Percentage increase = 100 × 6.9/9.0 ≈ 76.7%; the baseline is sham.
cards.quote: Percentage increase: 100 times 6.9 divided by 9.0 is 76.7 percent.
cards.section: A worked problem: the other half of the balance

cards.front: Why does a higher spontaneous EPSC frequency in dorsal-horn neurons not quantify how much more unpleasant a stimulus feels?
cards.back: It measures the frequency of excitatory synaptic events onto recorded neurons. Unpleasantness requires a different readout; reflexes and affective behaviours can dissociate.
cards.quote: a rise in the frequency of synaptic events onto these neurons.
cards.section: A worked problem: the other half of the balance

cards.front: A researcher combines increased EPSC frequency in Chen’s rats with KCC2 loss in Coull’s rats and claims both were measured in the same neurons. What would a direct test require?
cards.back: Measure excitatory input and KCC2 or E_anion in the same identified neurons, comparing injured and sham preparations. Rule: separate studies support a combined mechanism but do not establish co-occurrence within individual cells.
cards.quote: These EPSC measurements do not show a loss of inhibition in the same neurons:
cards.section: A worked problem: the other half of the balance

cards.front: A follow-up study restores adaptive immune cells to nerve-injured female mice that previously lacked them. If restoration reinstates the intact-female route, what response to a microglial inhibitor is predicted, and why?
cards.back: Resistance to the inhibitor should return under that assumption. Intact females were resistant, while females lacking adaptive immune cells became sensitive, showing that the route can switch with immune context.
cards.why: This restoration result is a prediction from the conditional mouse findings, not a reported experiment or a claim about immune routes in women.
cards.quote: Female mice lacking adaptive immune cells became sensitive to the glial inhibitor, so the pathway can switch.
cards.section: The twist: the chain depends on sex and compartment

cards.front: In mouse nerve-injury studies, how did the effect of systemic macrophage depletion differ from the sex-dependent response to spinal microglial inhibition?
cards.back: Macrophage depletion reduced mechanical hypersensitivity in both sexes. Spinal microglial inhibition reversed hypersensitivity in males but not intact females under the tested conditions.
cards.why: Ganglion macrophages expanded after injury. Immune mechanisms must be specified by cell type, sex and compartment.
cards.quote: Depleting macrophages throughout the body reduced mechanical hypersensitivity in both males and females,
cards.section: The twist: the chain depends on sex and compartment

cards.front: A sensory-neuron CSF1 blocker is proposed to prevent ganglion-macrophage expansion equally in male and female nerve-injured mice. What does the CSF1 deletion experiment predict about that proposal, and why?
cards.back: Equal effects are not supported. Deleting sensory-neuron CSF1 reduced expansion in males but not females, so a blocker may fail to prevent the female route in this model.
cards.quote: Deleting CSF1 from sensory neurons reduced that expansion in males but not in females.
cards.section: The twist: the chain depends on sex and compartment

cards.front: Systemic macrophage depletion reduces mechanical hypersensitivity in nerve-injured mice. Design a stronger test of whether ganglion macrophages specifically account for this effect.
cards.back: Compare ganglion-macrophage-specific depletion with a control that preserves those cells while testing the skin-cell contribution. Rule: systemic depletion also removed skin dendritic cells, so the original intervention cannot isolate the causal compartment.
cards.quote: Because it was systemic, it could not exclude a contribution from skin dendritic cells depleted at the same time,
cards.section: The twist: the chain depends on sex and compartment

cards.front: In nerve-injured male mice, silencing a tagged basolateral amygdala ensemble reduced escape and avoidance while preserving withdrawal reflexes. What distinction does the experiment support?
cards.back: Affective-motivational behaviours can be dissociated from reflex withdrawal in this model; withdrawal alone does not measure the full affective response.
cards.why: The result does not establish whether touch detection was preserved; that requires its own test. Scope is the tested male-mouse model and behaviours.
cards.quote: Affective-motivational pain behaviours fell, while the measured withdrawal reflexes were preserved.
cards.section: A reflex is not the hurt

cards.front: In rodent experiments, how did ACC stimulation show that descending control of spinal pain processing can facilitate transmission?
cards.back: ACC stimulation potentiated spinal excitatory transmission independently of the rostral ventromedial medulla; optogenetic activation of spinal-projecting ACC neurons sensitized pain-related behaviour in mice.
cards.quote: stimulation of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) potentiated spinal excitatory synaptic transmission in the rodent experiments,
cards.section: A reflex is not the hurt

cards.front: In the prospective subacute back-pain cohort, stronger baseline functional connectivity between which regions predicted persistence?
cards.back: Medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens.
cards.quote: Greater baseline functional connectivity between medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens predicted persistence,
cards.section: Predicting who stays in pain

cards.front: Why should “recovering” in the prospective back-pain cohort not be interpreted as “pain-free”?
cards.back: Classification used a 20 percent drop in pain intensity as the cutoff, so recovering patients could still have pain.
cards.quote: using a 20 percent drop in pain intensity as the cutoff, so recovering did not mean pain-free.
cards.section: Predicting who stays in pain

cards.front: {{c1::Nociceptive pain}} arises from actual or threatened non-neural tissue damage through nociceptor activation.
cards.quote: Nociceptive pain arises from actual or threatened non-neural tissue damage through nociceptor activation.
cards.section: Four words for pain, now that they mean something

cards.front: {{c1::Neuropathic pain}} is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system.
cards.quote: Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system.
cards.section: Four words for pain, now that they mean something

cards.front: What defines nociplastic pain in the IASP mechanistic descriptors?
cards.back: Altered nociception without clear evidence of nociceptor-activating tissue damage or a somatosensory nervous-system lesion or disease.
cards.quote: Nociplastic pain arises from altered nociception without clear evidence of either of those causes.
cards.section: Four words for pain, now that they mean something

cards.front: A patient has nociceptor-activating non-neural tissue damage and also meets criteria for nociplastic pain. Must one descriptor replace the other, and why?
cards.back: No; nociceptive and nociplastic descriptors can coexist. The presence of one mechanism does not require every component of the patient’s pain to have that mechanism.
cards.quote: The descriptors can coexist in one patient: nociceptive and nociplastic pain, for instance, can both be present.
cards.section: Four words for pain, now that they mean something

cards.front: Why is inflammatory pain not a fourth IASP mechanistic descriptor alongside nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain?
cards.back: It names a process: immune-system activation after tissue injury or infection. A process label can coexist with an IASP mechanistic descriptor.
cards.quote: It names a process, not a fourth IASP descriptor, so one patient can fit a process label and a mechanistic descriptor at once.
cards.section: Four words for pain, now that they mean something

cards.front: The back-pain connectivity study reports an ROC area of 0.83. If one persisting and one recovering patient are chosen randomly, how should their scores tend to rank?
cards.back: The persisting patient has higher connectivity about 83 percent of the time. This is pairwise discrimination, not 83 percent classification accuracy or an individual patient’s probability of persistence.
cards.quote: the persisting patient has the higher connectivity about 83 percent of the time.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A baseline brain-connectivity marker predicts back-pain persistence. What study would test whether changing the circuit changes persistence rather than merely improving prediction?
cards.back: Randomize an intervention that changes connectivity or the circuit, and measure later persistence. Rule: the observational prediction study establishes temporal information, not causation; randomized manipulation tests a causal effect.
cards.quote: an intervention that changes connectivity or the circuit in a randomized design, with persistence as the outcome.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A surgical ganglion study found spontaneous firing in 20 of 149 sampled neurons from 17 tumour patients. Would treating all 149 neurons as independent observations estimate the prevalence of misfiring in human sensory neurons?
cards.back: No. Rule: neurons sampled from the same person are clustered, and cultured surgical cells are a proxy rather than a population sample. Analyse the patient-level sampling and retain the preparation’s limits.
cards.quote: so 20 of 149 is not the fraction of human sensory neurons that misfire.
cards.section: Sampling in the human ganglion study

cards.front: For the rat EPSC recordings, sham SEM = 1.3 Hz and injured SEM = 1.6 Hz, each with n = 20 neurons. Using SD = SEM × √n, estimate the within-group standard deviations.
cards.back: Sham SD = 1.3 × √20 ≈ 5.8 Hz; injured SD = 1.6 × √20 ≈ 7.2 Hz. This describes neuronal spread; clustering within animals limits an independent-sample interpretation.
cards.quote: an SEM of 1.3 Hz with n = 20 means a standard deviation of about 1.3 times the square root of 20
cards.section: Animals, ages and spread in the cord recording

cards.front: In imaged male-mouse ACC CaMKIIa neurons, a stable population representation accompanied changing single-cell selectivity. Combined with BLA silencing results, does this justify searching for one neuron that constitutes pain?
cards.back: No. Rules: ACC population activity discriminated noxious stimuli from other sensory stimuli better than single-cell response identity did, while BLA silencing dissociated affective behaviours from withdrawal. These different preparations and readouts support distributed, separable functions, not one universal pain neuron.
cards.quote: the population representation stayed stable even as single-cell selectivity changed.
cards.section: How the anterior cingulate codes noxious stimuli

cards.front: How do opioid-receptor Gβγ signals reduce transmission at presynaptic and postsynaptic sites?
cards.back: Presynaptically, Gβγ inhibits voltage-gated calcium-channel opening. Postsynaptically, it activates GIRK potassium channels. Both reduce transmission.
cards.quote: presynaptic Gβγ inhibits the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, and postsynaptic Gβγ activates G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels,
cards.section: Tolerance is a separate topic

cards.front: Knock-in mice lack every tested opioid-receptor carboxyl-terminal phosphorylation site. Should this abolish morphine tolerance, and why?
cards.back: No. Analgesic tolerance was much reduced, but morphine tolerance persisted even after all tested sites were removed. Phosphorylation contributes without being the whole mechanism.
cards.quote: yet tolerance to morphine persisted even when every tested site was removed.
cards.section: Tolerance is a separate topic

cards.front: A NaV1.8 inhibitor, suzetrigine, is approved for moderate to severe acute pain in adults. Does that indication establish efficacy for persistent neuropathic pain?
cards.back: No. Evidence supporting an acute-pain approval does not establish efficacy in chronic pain; that indication needs its own evidence.
cards.quote: That approval does not establish efficacy in chronic pain.
cards.section: Tolerance is a separate topic
